resources.name: jaildeck API
resources.description:
Jail Deck JSON API collection for Insomnium / Insomnia (export format v4).

Import: Create -> Import -> File -> collections/insomnium.json

AUTHENTICATION IS MANDATORY (JD-003). Every request below returns 401 until you
authenticate; there is no unauthenticated mode, on any bind address.

  Browser session:  run Auth -> Login once. The cookie jar carries the session
                    from then on, so the other requests need no changes.
                    Set `password` in the environment first.

  API token:        jaildeck token add insomnium
                    Paste the token into `apiToken`, then send
                    Authorization: Bearer {{apiToken}}.
                    See Auth -> Bearer token (no cookie) for the shape.

The session cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Strict. Secure cookies are
accepted over http://localhost, so loopback works; a non-loopback plain-HTTP host
will not keep you logged in (see #27).

ENVIRONMENTS
  FreeBSD guest (SSH tunnel)  http://localhost:8888  jail=ottermq
  Local (fake adapter)        http://localhost:8889  jail=nginx

Jail Deck binds 127.0.0.1 by default (JD-002), so reaching a FreeBSD host needs a tunnel:
    ssh -N -L 8888:127.0.0.1:8888 <freebsd-host>

The fake-adapter environment uses a different port so it can run alongside that tunnel:
    JAILDECK_PORT=8889 JAILDECK_ADAPTER=fake ./bin/jaildeck

Adjust `jail` in each environment to a jail that exists there.

RESPONSE QUIRKS
  1. /jails keys are PascalCase (JID, Name, Status, Hostname, IP, Path) because the Jail struct has no json tags; /audit keys are snake_case.
  2. /host/readiness always sends `observed` and `remedy` as strings, empty when they do not apply, rather than omitting them.

MAINTAINING THIS FILE
IDs and __export_date are fixed so regenerating does not churn the diff. Re-exporting from the app rewrites both, so prefer editing this file directly.

resources.name: Auth
resources.description: Login, identity and logout. Run Login first: the cookie jar carries the session into every other request. Token authentication is the alternative and sets no cookie.

resources.name: Login
resources.description:
Response 200 with `{"authenticated": true}` and a Set-Cookie carrying an opaque session token — HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, Path=/, MaxAge 12h.

A wrong password returns 401 and sets no cookie. Verification is argon2id at 64 MiB and is deliberately serialised, so concurrent logins queue; past the queue depth the server returns 429 rather than accumulating work.

The password comes from the `password` environment variable. Set it before sending.

resources.name: Who am I
resources.description:
Response 200 with the authenticated principal, or 401 without a valid credential. The SPA calls this on boot and branches on 200 vs 401 — it cannot read the cookie and should not.

A session principal reports `kind: "session"` and `expires_at`. A token principal reports `kind: "token"`, its `name`, and omits `expires_at` because API tokens do not expire — they are revoked explicitly.

resources.name: Logout
resources.description:
Response 204. Deletes the server-side session and clears the cookie, so the old cookie returns 401 immediately.

Idempotent: logging out with no session, or an expired one, still returns 204 and still clears the cookie. That matters — requiring a valid session to log out would strand an operator holding a stale cookie.

resources.name: Bearer token (no cookie)
resources.description:
Token authentication, for scripting without a browser session. Create one with:

    jaildeck token add insomnium

The token is shown once; paste it into the `apiToken` environment variable.

The Authorization header takes precedence over the cookie, and a bad bearer token returns 401 rather than falling back to one — so this request fails cleanly even while a session is active. Token authentication sets no cookie, and is immune to CSRF by construction.

A revoked token stops working immediately: `jaildeck token revoke insomnium`.

resources.name: Jails
resources.description: Jail listing and lifecycle. Mutations are logged to the audit trail.

resources.name: Audit
resources.description: Operation history. Append-only JSON-lines file, filtered server-side.

resources.name: Errors & edge cases
resources.description: Deliberately invalid input, to see the real error surface.

resources.name: List jails
resources.description:
Merges `jls` (running) with `/etc/jail.conf` + `/etc/jail.conf.d/*.conf` (configured but stopped), so stopped jails appear too (JD-004). A missing jail.conf means zero jails, not an error.

Response 200: JSON array of jail objects.

NOTE: the Jail struct has no json tags, so keys are Go field names in PascalCase:
`JID`, `Name`, `Status`, `Hostname`, `IP`, `Path`. `Status` is `running` or `stopped`.

This is inconsistent with /audit, which uses snake_case. Worth reconciling before a UI depends on it.

On failure List does NOT go through toAppError, so an adapter error surfaces as 500 `{"error": "internal server error"}` with the detail only in the server log.

Example response:
  [{"JID":"4","Name":"ottermq","Status":"running","Hostname":"ottermq","IP":"","Path":"/usr/local/jails/containers/ottermq"}]

`IP` is empty because that jail uses `ip4 = inherit`, so it shares the host addresses rather than having one of its own. Do not treat an empty IP as an error.

resources.name: Root (redirects to /jails)
resources.description:
Returns 303 See Other with `Location: /jails`.

Insomnium follows redirects according to the global setting, so you will normally see the /jails response. Turn redirect-following off in this request's settings to observe the 303 itself.

resources.name: Start jail
resources.description:
`service jail start <name>` (JD-005). Idempotent: starting an already-running jail succeeds.

Response 200: the single updated jail object (same PascalCase keys as List).

Errors are `{"error": "..."}` with `Content-Type: application/json`.

resources.name: Stop jail
resources.description:
`service jail stop <name>`. Idempotent in the other direction.

Response 200: the single updated jail object.

Errors are `{"error": "..."}` with `Content-Type: application/json`.

resources.name: Restart jail
resources.description:
`service jail restart <name>`.

Response 200: the single updated jail object.

Errors are `{"error": "..."}` with `Content-Type: application/json`.

resources.name: Recent operations
resources.description:
Response 200: JSON array of audit entries, newest first, snake_case keys:
`timestamp`, `operation`, `target`, `command`, `exit_code`, `success`, plus `timed_out` (omitted when false) and `error` (omitted when empty).

Default limit 50, maximum 200.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Filter by operation + limit
resources.description:
`operation` is lowercased and matched exactly against the logged operation. Any value is accepted — audit records operations from every domain, so it does not keep a list of valid ones. An operation that was never logged simply matches nothing.

`limit`: non-numeric, empty, zero or negative fall back to 50; anything above 200 clamps to 200.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Failures only
resources.description:
`success` accepts only the strings `true` or `false`; any other value is ignored and no success filter is applied.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Filter by targets
resources.description:
`targets` is comma-separated; entries are trimmed and blanks discarded. A value that is only commas or whitespace means no filter.

Matching is case-sensitive, deliberately: FreeBSD jail names are case-sensitive, so `MyJail` and `myjail` are different jails. Only `operation` is normalised.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Unknown jail
resources.description:
Behaviour differs by adapter, which is itself worth knowing:

- `JAILDECK_ADAPTER=freebsd`: 404 `{"error": "jail not found"}` (the only place ErrJailNotFound is raised is freebsd/jail_helper.go).
- `JAILDECK_ADAPTER=fake`: the fake returns a plain error, so toAppError wraps it as 500 `{"error": "failed to start jail \"does-not-exist\": jail \"does-not-exist\" not found"}`.

So 404 is unreachable on the fake adapter.

resources.name: Invalid jail name
resources.description:
Names allow only `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - .` — anything else is rejected by NewJailName.

Response 400: `{"error": "invalid jail name \"bad name\""}`.

An empty name is also invalid but unreachable through routing, since `/jails//start` matches no route.

resources.name: limit above maximum
resources.description:
Clamps to 200 rather than erroring.

EMPTY RESULT: returns `[]`, not `null`. The log file is created lazily on the first mutating operation, relative to the process working directory.

resources.name: limit non-numeric
resources.description:
Falls back to the default of 50 rather than erroring.

EMPTY RESULT: returns `[]`, not `null`. The log file is created lazily on the first mutating operation, relative to the process working directory.

resources.name: Operation is case-insensitive
resources.description:
`START` is lowercased before matching, so it returns entries logged as `start`.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Timeouts only
resources.description:
`timed_out` accepts only the strings `true` or `false`; any other value is ignored and no timeout filter is applied — the same rules as `success`, which it shares a parser with.

Filters combine with AND. A timed-out operation is also a failure, so `timed_out=true` selects a subset of `success=false`.

In the response the key is omitted when false, so entries that did not time out carry no `timed_out` field at all.

An empty result is `[]`, not `null` — both when nothing matches and when the audit log does not exist yet (it is created on the first mutating operation).

resources.name: Unknown operation matches nothing
resources.description:
Returns `[]`, because no logged entry has operation `bogus`.

Before the audit filter was reworked, unknown operations were silently dropped and the request returned the unfiltered list instead.

resources.name: Host
resources.description: What the host can do, and the ZFS dataset layout jails are provisioned into. Only `PUT /host/layout` changes anything.

resources.name: Readiness report
resources.description:
Response 200: `{"capabilities": [...], "checks": [...]}`. Both arrays are always present and never `null`.

A check is `id`, `title`, `status` (`pass` | `fail` | `unknown`), `observed`, `detail`, `remedy` and `gates`. `remedy` is set on every `fail` and only there: an `unknown` carries none, because a check that could not observe the host cannot know what would fix it.

A capability is `id`, `title`, `status` (`ready` | `unavailable` | `unknown`) and `gated_by`. Any failing gate makes it `unavailable`, any unknown gate makes it `unknown`, and only then is it `ready`. The server derives this so that no client reimplements it.

Nothing in this path writes to the host. Jail Deck runs as root (JD-001); unprivileged, `devfs rule showsets` and `pfctl` refuse, and those checks answer `unknown` rather than `fail`.

resources.name: Jails dataset layout
resources.description:
Response 200: `{"pool", "datasets", "missing"}`. A dataset is `name`, `present`, `mountpoint` and `expected_mountpoint`, plus `mountpoint_taken_by` when it is missing and another dataset already holds its path.

409 when no pool can be chosen — several pools with `JAILDECK_ZFS_POOL` unset, a configured pool that is absent, no pool at all, or no ZFS (JD-021). The message is the `zfs_pool` check's own detail and remedy.

Reads only.

resources.name: Ensure the dataset layout
resources.description:
No request body: the layout is a singleton whose desired state is fixed (JD-016).

201 when something was created, 200 when everything was already in place — and then no `zfs create` ran at all. The body adds `changed` and `created` to the `GET` shape, read back from the system afterwards rather than from what the request believes it made (JD-011).

409, with nothing created, when a layout dataset exists but is mounted somewhere else, or when a missing one's expected mountpoint is already held by another dataset on any pool (JD-021). The body is the usual `{"error": "..."}` plus `"conflicts": [...]`, so a client can tell which dataset without parsing the message. Jail Deck will not move a mounted dataset or mount a new one over it: either may hold live jails.

Each `zfs create` writes one `create-dataset` audit entry, findable with `?targets=<dataset>`.

`jaildeck init` calls the same service method.

resources.name: Page backwards with a cursor
resources.description:
`before` is an RFC 3339 timestamp; entries strictly older than it are returned, newest first. Pass the `timestamp` of the oldest entry already received.

Composes with `operation`, `targets`, `success` and `timed_out`. The response stays a plain array, so a page that fills `limit` might still be the last one.

A cursor rather than an offset: the audit log is append-only and `newsyslog` rotates it, so an offset means something different between one request and the next.

resources.name: Unreadable cursor
resources.description:
Response 400. An unreadable `before` is rejected rather than ignored: a silently dropped cursor returns the first page again, so a client paging backwards would loop on it. An unreadable `limit`, by contrast, falls back to the default, because a wrong window is harmless.

The message names the format wanted rather than Go's layout string.
